design_detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019120220) of blinded, placebo-controlled acute caffeine challenge studies in adults with clinician-diagnosed panic disorder, with or without psychiatrically healthy controls. 10 within-person studies (1985–2015; 8 with randomized order, 2 with caffeine always given last), 244 people with panic disorder and 122 controls, single oral caffeine doses of 400 to about 750 mg (480 mg in 7 studies). Pooled outcomes: occurrence of panic attacks after caffeine in people with panic disorder versus controls (risk ratio, 6 studies) and self-rated anxiety change after caffeine (Hedges' g within each group and between groups, 6 studies). Placebo anxiety data were too sparse to pool, so the anxiety analyses are of change after caffeine alone.
can_establish: That in blinded laboratory challenges with single oral caffeine doses of 400 to about 750 mg, given at rest to adults with panic disorder who were off psychotropic medication, about half had a panic attack after caffeine and none after placebo, against about 2% of healthy controls after caffeine; and that self-rated anxiety rose more after caffeine in the panic disorder groups than in controls on average, with wide variation between studies.
cannot_establish: The effect of everyday amounts below 400 mg or any dose-response (almost all studies used 480 mg); effects in people taking medication or outside the laboratory; how much of the anxiety rise is due to caffeine rather than the test situation (placebo anxiety data in only 2 studies); a dependable pooled risk ratio (two incompatible versions are printed); or the mechanism.

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library to 14 October 2019, developed with a librarian, plus reference lists of included articles; English-language published original articles only, no date limit (Methods 2.3–2.4, pp. 23–24). Patients in the included studies were recruited from outpatient clinics in nine studies (not reported in one) (Results 3.2.2, p. 25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled or controlled clinical trials in adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician on DSM-III to DSM-5 or ICD-9/10 criteria; acute oral or intravenous caffeine against a placebo with identical or similar taste, given blind (double blinding and randomized order not required); anxiety on a continuous scale and/or panic attacks within 24 h; laboratory or clinical settings (Methods 2.2, p. 23). Excluded at full text: 3 without a placebo arm in a group, 2 without usable data, 1 without original data, 1 that told participants they were receiving caffeine, 1 with wrong outcomes (Results 3.1, p. 24). Studies of healthy people only were excluded, a disclosed deviation from the protocol (p. 23).
sample.demographics: Panic disorder groups of 7 to 83 people, mean ages 32.5 to 42 years (one study gives a range of 18–55), 50% to 79% women; control groups of 7 to 28, 36% to 73% women (Table 1, pp. 25–26).
sample.attrition: Within studies: 4 participants in two studies (Klein 3; Tancer 1), all from the caffeine condition (Results 3.7, p. 27). At review level: 18 full texts assessed, 8 excluded (p. 24).
sample.selection_effects: Small clinic samples tested off medication, at rest, in laboratories; English-language published reports only. The 10 studies come mainly from two research groups: four by Nardi and colleagues (refs 38–41) and four with Uhde among the authors (refs 34, 51, 53, 60), so they are not independent replications.

exposure.measurement: Caffeine and placebo given blind by the investigators in every study (Results 3.2.1, p. 25).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: single oral doses. 480 mg in 7 studies (capsules, caffeine base, or instant coffee, in three studies with sweetener tablets), 400 mg instant coffee in 1, and caffeine dosed by body weight in 2 (10 mg/kg caffeine citrate in ginger ale; 7 mg/kg in a caffeine-containing liquid; about 750 and 525 mg at 75 kg). Capsules in 2 studies, instant coffee in 5, other liquids in 3. Participants rested after intake; outcomes 30 to 240 min later (Results 3.2.3–3.2.4, p. 25; Table 1). The authors equate 480 mg with roughly 5 cups of brewed coffee at about 100 mg each (p. 28).
exposure.polysubstance: All included challenge studies were done during abstinence from psychotropic treatment (Discussion 4.2, p. 28). Alcohol, nicotine and other drug use are not reported in the main text; duration of caffeine abstinence and fasting before testing were extracted (p. 24) but appear only in Table S2 (not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Caffeine abstinence before testing was extracted but is not reported in the main text (Table S2, not read).

comparison.controls: Within-person placebo sessions in all 10 studies; psychiatrically healthy controls given the same challenge in 7. The pooled contrasts are people with panic disorder versus controls after caffeine, and change after caffeine within each group; caffeine versus placebo is described only narratively for anxiety.
comparison.matching: Not described at review level; age and sex by group in Table 1.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline anxiety sensitivity, respiratory subtype and ADORA2A genotype (examined in none of the included studies, p. 28); habitual caffeine use was extracted and said not to differ between groups (Table S2, not read; p. 28).

outcomes.instruments: Anxiety: visual analogue scales, Subjective Units of Distress, Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (state), Zung Anxiety Scale and an NIMH rating, self- or clinician-rated, at 30 to 240 min; panic attacks: proportion with a self- or clinician-reported attack (Table 1, pp. 25–26). Pooling in R (metafor, meta, dmetar): Hedges' g with a random-effects model, correlation between baseline and post-caffeine anxiety imputed as 0.5 with sensitivity analyses from 0.1 to 0.9; risk ratios by Mantel-Haenszel (Methods 2.8–2.11, p. 24).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard anxiety scales; a panic attack is defined by each study (self- or clinician-reported). Risk of bias with a modified Cochrane tool by both authors (Methods 2.7, p. 24; Fig. 2, p. 26).
outcomes.operationalization: Panicogenic effect: panic attack after caffeine (none occurred after placebo). Anxiogenic effect: rise in anxiety from before to after caffeine, and its difference between people with panic disorder and controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four primary pooled estimates (panic-attack risk ratio; anxiety change in each group; anxiety difference between groups), plus sensitivity analyses for the imputed correlation and time points (Table S3, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; study selection by both authors independently, extraction by one and checked by the other (pp. 24).

analysis.effect_sizes: Panic attacks after caffeine: 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51.1%) in 9 studies and 2 of 115 controls (1.7%); none after placebo in any study (p. 27). In the 6 studies with both groups, 69 of 128 (53.9%) versus 2 of 115 (1.7%); log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87), Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133 (p. 27). Editors' calculation: this is RR 32 (7.8 to 130); it is reproduced exactly by a Mantel-Haenszel RR without continuity correction with the Greenland-Robins interval, whose denominator rests on the 2 events in one control group; the forest plot (Fig. 4, p. 27) instead shows RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23), prediction interval 3.78 to 38.83, I² 0%. Risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation). In the 3 studies without controls, 52 of 109 (47.7%). Anxiety (6 studies, 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): change after caffeine g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) in panic disorder and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36) in controls; difference between groups g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), Q = 15.0, p = 0.01, I² 66.8% (20.7% to 86.1%) (p. 26); prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32 (Fig. 3, p. 27). Editors' recalculation from the forest-plot values: the Hartung-Knapp method with DerSimonian-Laird between-study variance reproduces 1.02 (0.08 to 1.96); without the study flagged as an outlier (Nardi 2009, g 2.51) it gives about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42019120220, registered 16 January 2019 and last updated 30 October 2019, after the search date of 14 October 2019. Two deviations are disclosed with reasons (mood outcome dropped; healthy-only studies excluded) (Methods 2.1, p. 23). The registry was not read. Undisclosed changes: the planned dose-response meta-regression was not possible (p. 24), the anxiety analysis became a caffeine-only pre–post analysis, and the panic estimator is described differently in Methods and Results.
analysis.selective_reporting: Two different pooled risk ratios are printed (text and abstract versus Fig. 4) without explanation of which is the primary result. The prediction interval for the anxiety difference, which crosses zero, appears only in the figure. No sensitivity analysis without the funnel-plot outlier is reported.
analysis.power: Not assessed; the authors call the number of studies small and ask for replication in larger challenge studies (Limitations, p. 29).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 9 small laboratory studies, about half of 237 medication-free adults with panic disorder had a panic attack within hours of a single oral dose of 400 to about 750 mg caffeine (mostly 480 mg), none had one after placebo, and 2 of 115 healthy controls had one after caffeine (difference about 52 percentage points in the studies with both groups). Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more in people with panic disorder on average, but this pooled difference (g 1.02) has a prediction interval from −1.27 to 3.32, shrinks to about 0.7 without one outlying study, and rests on change after caffeine without a placebo comparison.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that caffeine at doses roughly equal to 5 cups of coffee induces panic attacks in a large share of people with panic disorder and discriminates them from healthy adults, which the counts support; its pooled log RR (3.47) is one of two incompatible estimates in the paper. It also states that caffeine increases anxiety in patients and healthy adults at these doses (p. 22); the abstract's own limitations note that placebo anxiety data were lacking, and the discussion grades the anxiety effect as less certain (p. 28), but the within-group effects are uncontrolled pre–post changes. The statement that caffeine targets important mechanisms of panic disorder (p. 22) is not tested by the data. The clinical implication (inform patients, with the caveat that little is known below 480 mg) is appropriately qualified.

timeline.event: Charney et al. (1985): earliest included challenge study, 10 mg/kg caffeine in 21 people with panic disorder or agoraphobia with panic attacks and 17 controls, caffeine always last (ref 11); not read.
Nardi et al. (2007–2009): four included studies from one group, including the largest panic sample (83, no controls) and the outlying anxiety effect (g 2.51) (refs 38–41); not read.
Vilarim, Araujo and Nardi (2011): earlier systematic review of caffeine challenge in panic disorder without meta-analysis (ref 55); not read.
Masdrakis et al. (2015): latest included study, 400 mg instant coffee in 19 people with panic disorder (ref 59); not read.
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analytic estimate of caffeine's panicogenic and anxiogenic effects in panic disorder against healthy adults.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of caffeine challenge in panic disorder on the reading lists. The panic finding is consistent across studies (all six point the same way); its size as a ratio is uncertain because almost no control had an attack, so the proportions are the better summary. Doses below 400 mg have not been tested in panic disorder, as the authors say. The included studies were not read for this card.

funding.funder: Hjärnfonden (the Swedish Brain Foundation), Vetenskapsrådet (the Swedish Research Council), Riksbankens jubileumsfond (the Swedish Foundation for Humanities and Social Science Council), Åke Wibergs Stiftelse and Kjell och Märta Beijers stiftelse; the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (pp. 29–30).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (p. 30).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology and the Beijer Laboratory, Department of Neuroscience, Uppsala University; open access under CC BY (p. 22).

what_would_settle_it: A blinded, randomized dose-ranging challenge study (placebo and several doses including everyday amounts of 100 to 300 mg) in people with panic disorder and matched controls, with anxiety measured after placebo and caffeine on the same scales, repeated challenges to test reproducibility, and adequate samples of people on and off treatment.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, acute caffeine challenge, placebo and healthy-control comparisons, anxiety and panic outcomes specified (pp. 23).

Registered on PROSPERO on 16 January 2019 (searches covered records to 14 October 2019), with two deviations disclosed and justified (p. 23); last updated on 30 October 2019, after the search date; registry not read; changes in the anxiety analysis and the panic estimator are not presented as deviations.
Blinded placebo-controlled challenge studies (RCTs and CCTs), with a reason for restricting group comparisons to studies that tested both groups (pp. 23–24).

Six databases, librarian-built strategy (examples of terms given) and reference lists; but English-language published original articles only, without a stated reason, no grey literature or registries, and searches more than two years before publication. Applied as written per senior decision 21 (2026-10-25).
Both authors screened independently in Covidence (p. 24).
One author extracted and the other checked, disagreements resolved by discussion (p. 24); meets the consensus criterion as applied on sc_mcketin_2019.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the excluded studies are said to be in Table S1 (p. 24), a supplement not among the files; the text gives counts by reason.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives diagnosis, numbers, age, sex, caffeine vehicle, dose, order, anxiety measures and times, and panic counts; medication washout, habitual caffeine use, caffeine abstinence and the placebo vehicle are only in Table S2 (not read) or not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A modified Cochrane tool covering sequence generation, concealment, blinding, incomplete data and selective reporting, by both authors (p. 24); suitable for the caffeine-placebo element, but the pooled contrasts (panic disorder versus controls; change after caffeine) are not randomized and confounding was not assessed. Per-study judgments only in Fig. S3 (not read); Fig. 2 shows assessor blinding unclear in most studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The panic estimator is described as random-effects Mantel-Haenszel in the Methods and fixed-effect in the Results, continuity correction is said both to have been and not to have been applied, and the text's pooled log RR (3.47) differs from the forest plot's RR (12.12) without explanation (pp. 24, 26–27). The anxiety effects of caffeine are pooled as uncontrolled pre–post changes, and the interval method is not stated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by risk of bias (for example excluding the two fixed-order studies).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The risk-of-bias results (Fig. 2) are not discussed anywhere; the limitations cover the small number of studies, the imputed correlation, inexact instant-coffee doses and reproducibility (p. 29), not the risk of bias of the included studies.
I² with its interval and prediction intervals reported; the heterogeneity of anxiety effects is discussed, with no study features found to explain it (pp. 26, 28).

A close call: funnel plots for both outcomes, with one study flagged as unusually large for anxiety (p. 27); with 6 studies no test is possible, and the flagged study was not followed by a sensitivity analysis or a discussion of its impact.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding with funder role and a conflict declaration (pp. 29–30).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (4: English-only published articles without justification; 11: incompatible pooled risk ratios and inconsistent model description; 13: risk of bias never discussed), which gives critically low confidence under the AMSTAR 2 rules whatever item 7 turns out to be. This is a judgment about the pooled numbers, not about the raw counts, which are transparent: Table 1 lets a reader see that about half of the people with panic disorder and almost no controls had a panic attack after caffeine, and that nobody had one after placebo. Citable for: those proportions, the doses and conditions studied (single oral 400 to about 750 mg, at rest, off medication), and the absence of any study below 400 mg. Not citable for: a precise risk ratio, a placebo-controlled size of the anxiety effect, effects of everyday caffeine intake, or mechanisms.

key_findings.finding: Searches of six databases to 14 October 2019 (English-language published articles) gave 2647 records; after removing 754 duplicates, 1893 were screened, 18 read in full and 10 included.
key_findings.note: The search date is printed as October 142,019 (p. 23), a typesetting error for 14 October 2019.

key_findings.finding: All 10 included studies were within-person designs giving caffeine and placebo to everyone; 8 randomized the order and 2 always gave caffeine last; participants were blinded in all. They involved 244 people with panic disorder (from outpatient clinics in nine studies) and 122 healthy controls; three studies had no control group.

Caffeine was given orally in capsules (2 studies), instant coffee (5) or other liquids (3); seven studies used a fixed 480 mg, one 400 mg and two dosed by body weight (10 and 7 mg/kg, about 750 and 525 mg at 75 kg); participants rested afterwards and outcomes were measured 30 to 240 min after intake.
In the 9 studies reporting panic attacks, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51.1%) and 2 of 115 controls (1.7%) had a panic attack after caffeine; no study reported a panic attack after placebo.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 22); Results 3.5.2, 2nd paragraph (p. 27); Table 1 footnote 2 (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: In the 6 studies with both groups, 69 of 128 people with panic disorder (53.9%) and 2 of 115 controls (1.7%) had a panic attack after caffeine; pooled log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87), Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 22); Results 3.5.2, 1st paragraph (starts p. 26, estimate on p. 27)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: log RR 3.47 is RR 32 (7.8 to 130). Fig. 4 (p. 27, image) shows a different pooled RR, 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23), prediction interval 3.78 to 38.83, I² 0%; see reporting issues. Both controls with an attack were in one study (Nardi et al., ref 39: 2 of 28).

key_findings.finding: In the 3 studies without controls, 52 of 109 people with panic disorder (47.7%) had a panic attack after caffeine.

Anxiety after caffeine (6 studies, 121 people with panic disorder, 111 controls): pooled change g 1.94 (95% CI 1.19 to 2.69) in panic disorder and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36) in controls; greater rise in panic disorder, g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96); Q = 15.0, p = 0.01, I² 66.8% (20.7% to 86.1%).
key_findings.note: Fig. 3 (p. 27, image): prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; study estimates from 0.17 (Nardi 2008) to 2.51 (Nardi 2009). Editors' recalculation from the figure values without Nardi 2009: about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37).

key_findings.finding: Only 2 studies reported anxiety after placebo, so caffeine was not compared with placebo meta-analytically; all 5 studies that compared caffeine with placebo statistically found a greater rise in anxiety after caffeine, and the 4 of these with controls found larger effects in panic disorder.
The funnel plot flagged one study (Nardi et al., ref 38) as giving an unusually large anxiety effect, a possible bias; no small-study bias was seen for panic attacks.
Dose-response could not be analysed because 7 of the 10 studies used 480 mg and the range was 400 to 750 mg; the authors state that little is known about doses below 480 mg.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results and Implications (p. 22); Methods 2.11 (p. 24); Results 3.5.2 (p. 27)

key_findings.finding: Attrition was low: 4 participants in two studies, all from the caffeine condition.

All caffeine challenge studies in panic disorder to date were done at rest and during abstinence from psychotropic treatment; no apparent difference in habitual caffeine consumption between patients and controls was noted in the included studies.

Risk of bias (bar chart of the ten studies): sequence generation at high risk in about a fifth (the fixed-order studies); blinding of outcome assessors low risk in about a fifth, unclear in most and high in about a tenth; selective reporting unclear in about two fifths.
key_findings.note: Proportions read from the bar chart (an image) and approximate; per-study judgments are in Fig. S3 (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: Two incompatible pooled risk ratios for panic attacks: the abstract and text give log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) with Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133 (pp. 22, 27), while Fig. 4 (an image; values read from it) gives RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) with χ²(5) = 1.58, P = .90 and I² 0%. The Methods describe a random-effects Mantel-Haenszel estimate computed without continuity correction (p. 24); the Results describe a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel analysis using continuity correction (pp. 26–27).
reporting_issues.consequence: By the editors' calculation, the text's value (RR about 32) matches a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel estimate without continuity correction, which depends on the 2 control events in one study; the figure's value comes from continuity-corrected study ratios. Neither should be quoted as the size of the effect; quote the proportions (53.9% versus 1.7% in the same studies).

reporting_issues.issue: Study counts by outcome disagree: Results 3.2.4 says nine studies measured anxiety and eight panic attacks (p. 25), but the synthesis and Table 1 show nine with panic data and eight with anxiety data; Results 3.5.1 says only 2 studies reported placebo anxiety data and, two paragraphs later, only 3 (p. 26).
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts appear swapped or miscounted; use Table 1 and the synthesis (9 panic, 8 anxiety).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives Klein et al. as 5/17 (71%) with panic attacks in a group of 7; 5 of 7 is 71%, and the total of 121 of 237 requires 7. The Masdrakis row labels its 19 participants as healthy controls although they are people with panic disorder, and a template placeholder (YY.Y) is left in the Charney row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting errors; the pooled counts are consistent with n = 7 for Klein and with Masdrakis being a panic disorder group.

reporting_issues.issue: The prediction interval for the difference in anxiety rise between panic disorder and controls (−1.27 to 3.32) appears only in Fig. 3 (an image; values read from it); neither the abstract nor the text mentions that it includes zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement of increased sensitivity to caffeine-induced anxiety in panic disorder is presented without the uncertainty shown in the figure; together with the outlier, this makes the anxiety comparison weaker than the abstract suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list six risk-of-bias domains (p. 24), but Fig. 2 shows seven (adding other sources of bias); the panic counts are referred to Fig. 2, which is the risk-of-bias figure (p. 27).
